note: Two lists, and they say opposite things about their files.
`entries` is known FALSE POSITIVES of tools/release_screen.py's content sniffer.
An entry says: this file trips the sniffer, for this reason, and the reason is
not note text. Nothing here weakens the path rules — a file must already be
publishable by path to be sniffed at all.
`acknowledged` is the opposite claim: the hit is REAL, it is recorded, and it is
not fixed. It exists because a false-positive list is the wrong shape for a true
positive, and the alternatives are worse — deleting the file destroys an arm's
committed artefact to quiet a checker, and filing it under `entries` writes
'known false positive' next to something that is not one, in the exact place a
reader would go to check. Two extra fields are mandatory: `why_real` says why the
hit is genuine, `fixed_when` says what will clear it. An acknowledged violation
with no stated exit is a permanent exemption wearing a temporary label.
Neither list gates the exit code; `acknowledged` is printed in full on every run
instead, because it is a debt line rather than a status line. The gate that holds
it is this diff. Path rules are identical for both lists — an acknowledged entry
can no more name a corpus or sealed path than a false-positive one, and its
`sniff` is pinned the same way, so a DIFFERENT hit on an acknowledged file is
still UNEXPECTED and still fails. A path may appear in only one list.
`why_real` and `fixed_when` are committed prose and carry no surface form, span or
offset — the same rule as every other file here. Describing the shape of a
violation does not require quoting it.
Rules the screener enforces on this file, so they cannot be quietly relaxed:
- Literal paths only. No wildcards, no directory prefixes. The lesson of the
data/acquire/*.sh bypass is that a whitelist keyed on anything broader than
a filename stops naming what it permits.
- Nothing under data/ or sealed/, and nothing the deny rules cover. Those are
corpus and sealed paths; a sniffer hit on one of them is the alarm, not a
nuisance. data/README.md is excluded too, even though it is publishable: it
is the one file published out of a denied prefix, so it is the last file
that should be exemptible from the content check as well.
- `sniff` pins WHICH kind of hit is expected. A file allowlisted for Korean
prose that starts tripping the clinical-header pattern is reported as
unexpected, because that is a different fact about the file.
- `why` has to be a real sentence. An entry nobody can evaluate later is an
entry that gets renewed forever.
Reasons are written in English deliberately: Korean prose in this file would
trip HANGUL_PROSE and the allowlist would need an entry for itself.

acknowledged.why_real:
The first rule file written against the German layer of the mechanism vocabulary, and the first outside the es-meddocan series. 27 rule_ids, 8 findings, one unrecognised token each — no rule_id contributes two, so the finding count and the token count agree here. None of the eight is a person's name or a place name, which makes this a different population from the es-meddocan entries below and is the reason each was judged on 2026-09-21 rather than inherited. All eight are now REFUSED and this entry records violations and no pending work; no widening followed. Six were refused under step (1) of the expressibility test recorded beside the exclusion categories in release_screen.py — the token's mechanism sense is already sayable with accepted tokens, so refusing it takes nothing from the model. They are: a German preposition-article contraction in a date rule, which is the same refusal as the Spanish contraction on the iter5 entry and is sayable with the accepted preposition, article and particle tokens the German layer already holds; a German preposition of origin in a location rule, sayable with the accepted preposition that already means from; and four German compound nouns naming an identifier scheme's field label — a case number, a patient number, an insurance number and a file reference — each of which composes exactly from accepted tokens (case, patient, policy, record, number, id), with the German statutory-insurance abbreviation additionally already present in the code-token set. A seventh, the German word for colleague in a context-cue rule over the collegial letter frame, is refused on weaker ground and is recorded as such: the accepted role words doctor and arzt name the same mechanism approximately rather than exactly, so this is a near-synonym refusal of the kind the iter7 entry flagged as an honest edge, not a provably costless one. That caveat still stands and is not discharged by the eighth judgement.

The eighth was the one token left UNJUDGED when this entry was first written, and it was judged on 2026-09-21 and REFUSED. It is the two-letter abbreviation of the German word for doctor, in a prefix rule over the honorific. Two things had to be separated first, because this layer holds two abbreviation pairs on purpose (str beside strasse, plz beside postleitzahl) and together they look like a standing permission for 'the abbreviation of a word we already accept'. They are not one category: plz shortens the NAME OF A SCHEME and belongs with cp, nif and kvnr in the code-token set, while str is not a shortening at all but a DISTINCT SURFACE CUE, appearing compounded where the full form does not, so a rule matching one is not the rule matching the other and step (1) never applies. The doctor abbreviation is neither. It names no scheme — there is no ordering, digit count or check digit to describe, which is what separates it from iso — and the mechanism of its rule, an honorific marker preceding a name opening a NAME window, is sayable EXACTLY with accepted tokens: doktor in this layer, prefix, title and abbrev in the English vocabulary, composing to doktor_abbrev_prefix_name if the author wants the abbreviation recorded in the name. So step (1) refuses it at zero cost, and this is the same refusal as iter8's abbreviation of 'international' rather than a conflict with it: opening 'abbreviation of a word we already hold in full' is the strictly worse vocabulary that entry named. gaz is not a counter-case, because gazetteer is a mechanism word and a naming.yaml layer axis value, so gaz shortens the name of a mechanism category while doktor is a language-layer commonplace. It is worth recording what this refusal is NOT: the token cannot point at an individual, and it is exactly the honorific category the exclusion notes admit when they say a title is a marker that precedes a name and not the name. The judgement order puts expressibility before category membership, so it ended at step (1) and never reached that question. The reasoning is recorded in release_screen.py beside the judgement order, not only here, because the next German arm writing the same token is repeating this judgement rather than raising a new one.
acknowledged.fixed_when: Not in this arm, and the reason is not a frozen prompt. This is a single-call arm: there is no round 2 to write a better name in, so the file is final the moment it is scored and nothing in the arm can repair it. The pin stays at EIGHT, because the token that could have moved it was refused rather than admitted — the count was written to break in exactly one way, by judging the doctor abbreviation, and judging it as a refusal is the branch that leaves the count standing and turns this entry into a clean set of refusals. The near-synonym caveat on the colleague token is the only soft edge left, and it is recorded above rather than resolved: refusing a near-synonym has low cost, not provably zero.
